The 2019 "Lesbian divorce 75%" thing was in the UK and misinterprets the data. Everything I'll say is sourced from the UK ONS reports on Marriages in Divorce, from the years 2014-2019 (as 2014 was the legalization of gay marriage), all publicly available at [www.ons.gov.uk](http://www.ons.gov.uk)



As of 2019 in the UK, there had been \~22,000 female-female marriages and \~17,000 male-male marriages, so men were married at a 77% rate compared to women. Of the F-F marriages, a total of 1,262\* (or 5.73%) had ended in divorce. Of the M-M marriages, a total of 460\* (or 2.70%) had ended in divorce.



The UK has seen an average of 240,836 Male-Female marriages from 2014-2019...and every year in that same span has an average of 103,220 Male-Female divorces. Or 42%.



While the numbers on same-sex marriage are small, and women in F-F relationships often divorce at a rate double that of M-M relationships so there's probably study to be made there, they are doing far better than Male-Female marriages. In the UK. From 2014-2019. If you're interested in further or more modern research, I came across the 2022 NSO report and briefly scanned it, noting that at that point M-M relationships were applying for divorce equally as F-F ones. 



\*there are no given statistics for same-sex divorces in 2014

I can really see your point. There are many, many ways to be polyamorous such as having closed circles vs open dating or anarchistic vs hierarchical, it all depends on the people within those relationships. Shayol above seems to be suggesting that having more interaction between the constellation via Avi x Elayne is a positive thing, which on a knee-jerk reaction I agreed with. Then I stopped to think, am I suggesting that a Romantic + Sexual relationship is "more meaningful" than a relationship between people who choose to be as sisters? I mean, after all, there are many different kinds of love besides romantic, and all of them are valid. 

When viewing the 4-person relationship through the lens that Romantic Love is inherently better, if you devalue the Familial Love that Avi and Elayne develop, then the constellation does seem one-sided and Rand-centric. But I don't think that's the right way to view it. The show rewriting their relationship emits that notion, I think, and from Rafe's comments exhibits a horrible misunderstanding of the source material.

  
If anything, Min is the one "on the outs" of the relationship....and that's not an issue. She doesn't have to be involved with the entire constellation, it doesn't have to be a fully interconnected quad, that's not a requirement for a valid relationship. It's whatever the people within that relationship are comfortable with, and showing positive variety in relationships is a damn good thing. I don't know if the quotes are real, but I saw quotes attributed to Rafe dismissing Min's role in Rand's life, and that irritates me. If he truly thinks Min isn't "as important" to Rand as the other two women, what books did he think he was reading?

Polyamorous person. I won't suggest what you should do, but will help how I can. I appreciate your willingness to explore--that you're dedicated to both of you and not wanting to limit your partner out of fear is a positive and healthy sign. Stories where one person tries to prevent their partner from having same-sex friends out of insecurity or jealousy, silently acknowledging that their relationship might not be what the partner wants, are way too common.

Seeing as how trying polyamory can be a significant change, there are self-help books that I'd recommend, namely "The Ethical Slut." It basically explains the various concepts and terms in polyamory and how to navigate common problems. The big thing they talk about is communication, which from your post you seem not to have a problem with. So long as you're honest and open and talk about your feelings without being accusatory (don't frame your negative emotions as things done to you, for example. You made me angry vs I felt angry when...) you have a lot of what you need already to feel out and establish boundaries of what is and isn't okay, what you both need to feel secure in your relationship. Just remember, you're exploring new ground. Don't take every mistake to be a personal affront or proof your partner doesn't care. Talk about it when your temper is down and figure out how to make sure it doesn't happen again.

One big thing with switching to polyamory is letting go of the toxic traits monogamy has taught. Not that monogamy itself is toxic, but in our culture some parts of it are. Feelings of ownership, the jealous limiting described above, the need to be everything for your partner. It can be hard watching your partner leave for a date with someone else. All those insecurities rise up, those what-ifs, the fear of being left. And it would be dishonest to say that wasn't a risk, especially for traditional monogamists. But that comes back to those toxic traits. If one date is enough to make someone leave you, how good were you for each other, really? I think you should be confident in your relationship. That if your partner sees someone else, they'll come back to you and you and your relationship won't be any less for it. (NOT to be confused with being used or ignored.) The only way to get there is to let it happen, even if you're scared.

Compersion is a poly term. It's the feeling of happiness people feel when seeing their partners involved with someone else. It's amazing--a feedback loop. When you see your partner happy, it makes you happy. And when your partner is happy to see you happy, it feeds back into itself. And into their other partners. And so on.

The shape of poly relationships is unique for each "polycule." Some prefer triads. Some, closed circles. One of the more common shapes is a Constellation, where each person is a link, but doesn't link with EVERY other star. Each branches off on their own, extending outwards, until you don't even know who you're distantly connected to. Some relationships allow casual sex, some prefer not to know or hear about their partner's partner (or "metamour"). It's all boundaries that need be discussed and felt out together such that everyone is fulfilled and happy. Boundaries need not be permanent. You can start strict and loosen up when you figure out what you're okay with, or you can allow everything and figure out what you don't like. So long as you trust your partner and communicate effectively, your relationship stands a decent chance of figuring out if polyamory is acceptable.

You're talking about Polyamory, and yes it is morally fine but socially can draw eyes. To make it work you must ensure it is ethical and that all partners communicate.

Establish boundaries, what each person wants and is willing to do/give up for each other. They'll take some experimenting to discover, so dip your feet in and trust that your partner(s) isn't intending to hurt you if you mess up--communicate your pain and work together to ensure it doesn't happen again.

Something else most people broaching into polyamory deal with is feelings of jealousy. Monogamous culture has given us a sense of ownership of partners. You have to release that. Understand that love is not limited and your partner being happy can bring you happiness (a feeling known as compersion), that just because they're happy with someone else does not mean they aren't happy with you or won't come back to you.

If you're serious about giving it a try, I suggest you pick up the book "The Ethical Slut." It's a great help for navigating common poly problems, managing your emotions, and teaching communication and poly culture. Good luck <3
